title: Grilled Leg Of Lamb
description:
Place the onion, garlic, ginger, and jalapeño pepper in the food processor, and process until the mixture is pureed.
Add the soy sauce, honey, and peanut oil, and mix just enough to combine.
If time allows, place the meat and marinade in a Ziploc bag, and refrigerate (up to overnight).
When ready, preheat oven to 180 degrees.
Grill the meat, slathered with the marinade, over a hot surface for about 4 to 5 minutes per side, until the meat is nicely browned.
Put the meat in the oven and let it slowly cook in its own juices for at least 30 minutes, maybe up to an hour, as the internal temperature rises to around 130 degrees.
Carve the lamb into slices (no sinew and no waste!) and put on a warmed plate with the accumulated juices.
This recipe is from one of the best cookbooks that we own: Jacques Pepin’s “The Art of Cooking.” The two volumes of this set cover almost every variety of food (from a French perspective), and show step-by-step instructions, with pictures and commentary, on how to prepare the dishes. The book’s format is one that we’ve mimicked here, but not with the wonderful detail that he had.
If I ever had a year off and wanted a good cooking/learning project, I might work my way through this book, or Julia Child’s “The Art of French Cooking” or maybe Thomas Keller’s “The French Laundry Cookbook” (where we’ve spent a lot of time preparing for the Women’s Resource Dinner in 2009).
This lamb recipe is actually surprisingly easy and delicious (though in this version, I don’t have you deboning the whole leg of lamb, which Jacques gives instruction on.)
Grilled Leg of Lamb Robert

ingredients: 1 piece of ginger (same amount as garlic)
directions: With a very sharp knife, trim away any lumps of fat and sinew that are visible underneath and on top of the lamb.
What you want to end up with is a collection of cleaned meat, all about the same thickness.

If you have a thicker separate piece, you can butterfly it by slicing in about an inch deep (with the grain) and spreading the meat open, maybe pounding it with the base of your palm or a heavy pan to flatten it out.
